newsitem.title: UK: Woolwich B/S disappointed by draft law.
newsitem.headline: Woolwich B/S disappointed by draft law.

text.p: The Woolwich Building Society said on Wednesday it is disappointed that the government has not taken into account its "serious concerns" on the timing of a draft new law on building societies.

The Woolwich, which has assets of just under 30 billion stg, said that its decision to convert to bank status and float on the stock exchange next year was taken on the basis of existing legislation which gave converting building societies immunity from takeover for five years.

"Had our board known when it took the decision to convert that this (change in the law) was even a possibility, then we might have chosen to convert in a different way," a spokeswoman for the Woolwich told Reuters.
The Woolwich says that when it published an earlier draft of the bill, the Treasury excluded even debate on the five-year immunity provisions, suggesting that these would not be changed.
The spokeswoman said that alternative arrangements could have included a longer conversion period during which the Woolwich could have made acquisitions.

Under the government's new draft, converting societies will lose their five-year immunity if they buy another financial institution. This does not include the purchase of mortgage assets or joint ventures.

In common with other converting societies, the Woolwich wanted the government to differentiate between hostile and agreed takeovers when setting the new rule but the Treasury has said this was unworkable.

The Woolwich spokeswoman said the society did welcome a government compromise on a rule which would have allowed the shareholders of a converted society to waive the immunity at a special general meeting by a simple majority.
The Treasury is now proposing that 75 percent of voting shareholders have to approve any such move.
"It appears that this Bill has been rushed out and we will lobby to ensure that it is suitably amended on its way through Parliament," the Woolwich said.

It is highly uncertain that the Bill will become law during this parliamentary session as a general election is due by May 1997 and the bill was not included in the government's original legislative agenda.
